terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to see whether the team is ready to go.

tasks.title: Is there enough crew?
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `ready_to_go.py`, make a variable called `enough_crew`: `True` when `crew_ready` is `crew_needed` or more, `False` otherwise. Print it to see it.

Check runs your file with other crews, including one with exactly the crew needed, and expects `True` or `False` itself.
nextSteps: Read the team's state near the top of the file.
Pick the comparison that means "or more".
Make `enough_crew` from that comparison of the two names.
hints: A comparison is already True or False. You can store it in a variable as it is.
There are two comparisons for "bigger": one leaves out the equal case and one includes it. The task includes it.
The line has the shape `enough_crew = crew_ready ... crew_needed`, with "bigger than or equal to" in place of the dots.

tasks.title: Is the radio on the team channel?
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, make a variable called `on_channel`: `True` when `radio_channel` is the same as `team_channel`, `False` otherwise. Print it to see it.

Check tries channels that are the same, channels far apart and channels one apart.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on `=` and `==`.
Pick the comparison that asks whether two values are the same.
Print it, then change `radio_channel` at the top to see it change.
hints: You are asking a question about two values, not storing one in the other.
One `=` stores a value. Asking whether two values are the same takes two.
The line has the shape `on_channel = radio_channel ... team_channel`, with the comparison for "the same as" in place of the dots.

tasks.title: Ready to go?
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, make a variable called `ready_to_go`: `True` only when there is enough crew (`enough_crew`), the radio is on the team channel (`on_channel`) and the stretcher is packed (`stretcher_packed`). Print it to see it.

Check starts Task 3 from `enough_crew` and `on_channel` as Tasks 1 and 2 should make them, and tries every one of the three missing in turn.
nextSteps: List the three things that must all be true.
Pick the word that is True only when both sides are.
Join the three names with it.
Print it, then set `stretcher_packed` to `False` at the top and run it again.
hints: One thing missing is enough to keep the team at the base.
Python has `and`, `or` and `not`. Only one of them needs every side to be True.
The line has the shape `ready_to_go = enough_crew ... on_channel ... stretcher_packed`, with the same word in both gaps.

videos.title: True, False, and, or, not and None

tasks.title: Is the casualty's name known?
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, `casualty_name` is `None` until someone gives the team a name. Make a variable called `name_known`: `False` when `casualty_name` is `None`, `True` when it holds a name. Print it to see it.

Check tries no name and two different names.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on None.
Find the words Python uses to ask whether something is None.
Turn the question round: you want True when it is not None.
Print it, then put a name in `casualty_name` at the top and run it again.
hints: None is not text and not zero. It is Python's value for "nothing here yet".
Python asks about None with `is` rather than `==`, and `not` turns an answer round.
The line has the shape `name_known = casualty_name is ... None`, with the word that turns the answer round in the gap.
